```{r}
# Part A. 
# A conditional statement lets R choose what to do based on whether a condition is TRUE or FALSE. Run each example, then change the values to see the output change.

# Example A: if ... else. Choose between two outcomes for a single value.

score <- 89

if (score >= 75) {
  print("Passed")
} else {
  print("Failed")
}
```
```{r}
# B. if ... else if ... else. Use it when there are more than two outcomes. R checks from top to bottom and stops at the first condition that is TRUE.

score <- 95

if (score >= 90) {
  print("Excellent")
} else if (score >= 80) {
  print("Good")
} else if (score >= 75) {
  print("Fair")
} else {
  print("Needs Improvement")
}
```
```{r}
# C. ifelse() for a whole vector. if works on one value at a time. ifelse() checks every element of a vector at once, which is what you need for a column of data.

scores <- c(88, 67, 93, 85, 77)
ifelse(scores >= 75, "Passed", "Failed")
```
```{r}
# D. combining conditions. Use & when both conditions must be true and | when at least one must be true.

age <- 20
score <- 85

if (age >= 18 & score >= 75) {
  print("Qualified")
} else {
  print("Not Qualified")
}

age <- 16
score <- 85

if (age >= 18 | score >= 75) {
  print("Qualified")
} else {
  print("Not Qualified")
}
```

# Question 2. Set age <- 17. Use if ... else if ... else to print "Child" for ages below 13, "Teenager" for 13 to 19, and "Adult" for 20 and above.

marks <- c(45, 88, 73, 100, 62)

# Question 4. Predict the output of the code below before you run it. Then run it and explain, in a comment, why you got that result.

x <- 10
if (x > 5) {

} else if (x > 8) {

```{r}
# Question 5. What is the difference between if and ifelse()? When would you choose each one?
# Answer: `if` is used when you want to check a single condition and choose between two actions, while `ifelse()` is used when you want to check multiple values at once and return results in a vector. I would use `if` for a single decision and `ifelse()` when working with a group of values.
```
```{r}
# Part C. You are the data assistant of Mabini National High School. The registrar gave you students_grades.csv, which holds quiz, midterm, and final exam scores and attendance for 15 students. Your job is to compute each student’s final grade, decide who passed, assign grade remarks, flag students at risk, identify honors candidates, and send the cleaned results back to the registrar as CSV files.

# Question 6. Import the file safely.
df <- read.csv("students_grades.csv")

# b. Use if ... else to check that the file exists before importing it.
file <- "students_grades.csv"

if (file.exists(file)) {
  grades_df <- read.csv(file)
  print(head(grades_df))
} else {
  print("File does not exist.")
}
```
```{r}
# c. Inspect the data. first 6 rows number of rows and columns column names and data types basic statistics per column number of missing values per column

students_grades <- read.csv("students_grades.csv")

head(students_grades, 6)

nrow(students_grades)
ncol(students_grades)
dim(students_grades)

names(students_grades)

str(students_grades)

summary(students_grades)

colSums(is.na(students_grades))

```
```{r}
# d. Answer the following:
# How many rows and columns does grades have? - 15 rows and 7 columns.
# Which column contains missing values (NA), and how many? - Midterm column has 1 missing value.
# What is the data type of the Section column? - Character (chr).
# What are the lowest and highest Attendance values? - Lowest: 70 Highest: 100
```
```{r}
# e. Check the grades should have 15 rows, 7 columns, and exactly one NA.

grades <- read.csv("students_grades.csv")

head(grades, 6)
nrow(grades)
ncol(grades)
dim(grades)
names(grades)
str(grades)
summary(grades)
colSums(is.na(grades))
nrow(grades) == 15 && ncol(grades) == 7 && sum(is.na(grades)) == 1

```
```{r}
# f1. Compute the final grade.** Any arithmetic with NA gives NA, so the student with the missing midterm will have NA as a final grade. This is expected.
grades$Final_Grade <- (grades$Quiz * 0.30) + (grades$Midterm * 0.30) + (grades$Final * 0.40)

grades$Final_Grade
```
```{r}
# f2.  Pass or fail.** Check for NA first, because NA >= 75 gives NA, not TRUE or FALSE.
grades$Result <- ifelse(is.na(grades$Final_Grade), "Incomplete", ifelse(grades$Final_Grade >= 75, "Passed", "Failed"))

grades$Result
```
```{r}
# f3. Grade remarks.** Replace each ___ with the correct cutoff or label, then change eval=FALSE to eval=TRUE in the chunk header.
grades$Remarks <- ifelse(is.na(grades$Final_Grade), NA,
                  ifelse(grades$Final_Grade >= 90, "Excellent",
                  ifelse(grades$Final_Grade >= 85, "Very Good",
                  ifelse(grades$Final_Grade >= 80, "Good",
                  ifelse(grades$Final_Grade >= 75, "Fair",
                  "Needs Improvement")))))
```
```{r}
# f4. Attendance flag.** Write one ifelse() statement that creates a column AttendanceFlag with "At Risk" when Attendance is below 80 and "OK" otherwise.
grades$AttendanceFlag <- ifelse(grades$Attendance < 80, "At Risk", "OK")
```
```{r}
# f5.  Honors candidates.** Write one ifelse() statement that creates a column Honors with "Yes" or "No". Use & to require both a final grade of 90 or higher and attendance of 90 or higher. Students with a missing final grade must get "No". Hint: use !is.na(grades$FinalGrade) as the first condition.
grades$Honors <- ifelse(!is.na(grades$Final_Grade) & grades$Final_Grade >= 90 & grades$Attendance >= 90, "Yes", "No")
```
```{r}
#f6. if ... else if inside a loop.** ifelse() works on a whole column, but a plain if handles one value at a time. To use if on a column you must loop over the rows.
grades$Remarks <- character(nrow(grades))

for (i in 1:nrow(grades)) {
  if (is.na(grades$Final_Grade[i])) {
    grades$Remarks[i] <- "Incomplete"
  } else if (grades$Final_Grade[i] >= 90) {
    grades$Remarks[i] <- "Excellent"
  } else if (grades$Final_Grade[i] >= 85) {
    grades$Remarks[i] <- "Very Good"
  } else if (grades$Final_Grade[i] >= 80) {
    grades$Remarks[i] <- "Good"
  } else if (grades$Final_Grade[i] >= 75) {
    grades$Remarks[i] <- "Fair"
  } else {
    grades$Remarks[i] <- "Needs Improvement"
  }
}
```
```{r}
# f7. Now try if (grades$FinalGrade >= 75) print("Passed") on its own in the Console. Explain the error or warning R gives and why the loop version avoids it.
if (grades$FinalGrade >= 75) print("Passed") # if handles one value at a time, while a for loop allows us to process every student's grade individually.
```
```{r}
# f8. Summarize your results.** Then write in comments how many students passed, how many are At Risk, and how many are honors candidates. Compare with a seatmate.
# The dataset contains 15 students. Based on the computed final grades, 10 students passed, 4 students are At Risk because their attendance is below 80, and 4 students are honors candidates. One student has an incomplete final grade because of a missing midterm score.
```
```{r}
# Part D.
# Question 7.
# a. Export the full processed table.** The argument row.names = FALSE stops R from adding an extra numbering column.
write.csv(grades, "processed_grades.csv", row.names = FALSE)
```
```{r}
# b. Export the at-risk students.** The file is written only when there is at least one at-risk student.
at_risk <- grades[grades$AttendanceFlag == "At Risk", ]

if (nrow(at_risk) > 0) {
  write.csv(at_risk, "at_risk_students.csv", row.names = FALSE)
}
```
```{r}
# c. Export the honors list.
# 1. Create a data frame honors with only the rows where Honors is "Yes".
# 2. Keep only these columns: StudentID, Name, Section, FinalGrade, Attendance. Hint: grades[rows_condition, c("StudentID", "Name")].
# 3. Use an if ... else statement to export it as honors_list.csv, or print a message if the list is empty.
honors <- grades[grades$Honors == "Yes", c("StudentID", "Name", "Section", "Final_Grade", "Attendance")]

if (nrow(honors) > 0) {
  write.csv(honors, "honors_list.csv", row.names = FALSE)
} else {
  print("No honors candidates found.")
}
```
```{r}
# d. Verify your exports. Never assume a file was written correctly. Read it back and compare. 
processed_check <- read.csv("processed_grades.csv")
at_risk_check <- read.csv("at_risk_students.csv")
honors_check <- read.csv("honors_list.csv")

identical(processed_check, grades)
identical(at_risk_check, at_risk)
identical(honors_check, honors)

file.exists("processed_grades.csv")
file.exists("at_risk_students.csv")
file.exists("honors_list.csv")
```

```{r}
# b. Use nested ifelse() statements. Test the missing grade first, then Full, then Partial
grades$Scholarship <- ifelse(is.na(grades$Final_Grade), "Pending",
                      ifelse(grades$Final_Grade >= 95 & grades$Attendance >= 90, "Full",
                      ifelse(grades$Final_Grade >= 85 & grades$Attendance >= 90, "Partial",
                      "None")))
```
```{r}
# c. Select students whose Scholarship is "Full" or "Partial". Hint: %in% c("Full", "Partial").

                      ifelse(grades$Final_Grade >= 95 & grades$Attendance >= 90, "Full",
                      ifelse(grades$Final_Grade >= 85 & grades$Attendance >= 90, "Partial",
                      "None")))
```

```{r}
# Question 10
# Why did you check is.na() before comparing the final grade to a number?
# I checked is.na() first because missing values cannot be compared properly with numbers. It prevents errors and allows students with missing grades to be marked as Incomplete.
# In Task 3.2, what would happen if the Failed condition were placed before the Incomplete condition?
# Students with missing grades might not be properly identified as Incomplete because comparisons involving NA return NA, not TRUE or FALSE. Checking Incomplete first ensures missing grades are handled correctly.
# When is ifelse() the better choice than if ... else, and when is if ... else better?
# ifelse() is better when applying conditions to an entire column or vector at once. if ... else is better when checking one value at a time, especially when used inside a loop.
# Why is it useful to read an exported CSV back into R?
# Reading an exported CSV back into R helps verify that the file was saved correctly and that the data, columns, and values are preserved. It helps detect missing or incorrect information before using or sharing the file.
```
